biography.text: Usha Sanyal situates Ahmad Riza Khan (1856–1921) in the learned society of late-nineteenth-century North India. She describes him as born into a well-to-do, learned Pathan family in Bareilly; educated at home by his father, Naqi Ali Khan; and known by the 1880s among North Indian ulama for rational sciences (maʿqulat), including logic, mathematics, and Islamic law. His writings became an intellectual basis for the Ahl-e Sunnat movement. Sanyal presents his scholarly and Qadiri Sufi roles together, while identifying fatwa-writing as his most important scholarly activity. This account distinguishes historical context from devotional childhood stories and unsupported work-count claims.
gaps: Read Sanyal's full biography and primary Urdu biographical works for a fuller chronology, family, teachers, travel, and work catalogue.
Verify exact birth/death dates and distinguish year-level evidence from later day-level dates.

timeline.text: Sanyal gives 1856–1921 as the life span and places Ahmad Riza among North Indian ulama by the 1880s. Siddiqui lists four astronomy-related works dated 1919, 1920, 1920, and 1921. For Fauz-i-Mubin, introductory matter in a 2005 English rendering reports 1919 while Siddiqui lists 1920; the original Urdu imprint has not been inspected, so that book date remains unresolved.
gaps: Inspect Urdu first editions' title pages, colophons, and any magazine antecedents to distinguish composition, serial publication, and book publication dates.

fields.text: The evidence identifies four writings associated by Siddiqui with the 1919 planetary-alignment episode: Muʿīn-i-Mubīn, Fauz-i-Mubin, al-Kalimah al-Mulhamah, and Nuzūl-i-Āyāt-i-Furqān. Sanyal independently characterizes Khan as learned in rational sciences, including logic and mathematics, but does not assess these astronomy treatises. The detailed passage study here covers only the reported preface and a geometric argument in Fauz-i-Mubin. The dossier records historical claims; it does not validate the physical reasoning or present a stationary-Earth conclusion as modern astronomy.
gaps: Collate the Urdu originals with the cited translations and record printed Urdu pages, diagrams, and technical terminology.
Reconstruct selected arguments from original diagrams and proofs; distinguish mathematical premises from physical inferences.
Read the 2026 Urdu study on mathematical works before summarizing its abstract claims.
Check the 1919 newspapers cited by Siddiqui and independently calculate the planetary configuration before assessing the Porta episode.

legacy.text: Sanyal situates Khan's writings and leadership in the Ahl-e Sunnat movement and the wider colonial-era North Indian scholarly milieu. Siddiqui's article describes a four-work astronomy sequence but calls itself introductory and says detailed analysis is not its main focus. A separate 2026 Urdu article advertises a broader survey of mathematical writings, but only its abstract was inspected and none of its findings are adopted here. No claim of scientific correctness, originality, or priority is made.
gaps: Review independent scholarship and the new 2026 mathematical study; inspect editions, reception, and calculations with qualified historical and scientific review.

investigations.title: The argument structure of Fauz-i-Mubin and its reported geometric reasoning
investigations.field: History of astronomy / history of science in South Asia
investigations.historicalProblem: What does the available evidence establish about the structure and mathematical style of Fauz-i-Mubin, and what remains unverified until the Urdu text is examined?
investigations.historicalContext: Siddiqui situates the work amid early twentieth-century debates over Earth's motion and reports that a 1919 planetary-alignment prediction prompted a series of writings by Ahmad Raza Khan. His paper describes the work as a polemical response drawing on contemporary scientific vocabulary, geometry, logic, and religious sources. The newspaper story, chronology, and the work's arguments must be independently checked rather than taken from a sympathetic introduction as settled fact.
investigations.method: Read Siddiqui's complete article and inspected the referenced 2005 English rendering's edition matter and cited passage locator. Checked Rekhta's catalogue metadata for an Urdu-language 197-page copy contributed by Rampur Raza Library, but its page images were gated after the free allowance. Recorded Siddiqui's translations as mediated quotations; did not transcribe or translate Urdu, reconstruct the diagram, test the physical claims, or independently verify the 1919 newspaper reports.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: The author-preface excerpt as quoted by Siddiqui divides the arguments into 12, 50, and 43 items, whose stated total is 105. A later translated excerpt uses equal segments and comparisons of distances in a geometric diagram, then draws a physical inference about attraction, repulsion, and Earth's motion. Only the count sum was arithmetically checked; the geometry, translation, and physical inference were not independently tested.
investigations.reportedResult: The available evidence supports a source-linked description of how one 2023 article reports the treatise's self-described structure and one translated geometric argument. It does not establish the original edition date, the exact Urdu wording, the soundness of the calculations, or the truth of the work's stationary-Earth conclusion.
investigations.whatWasNew: This dossier converts a weakly documented catalogue entry into a reviewable research record with distinct mediation, edition, and evidence limits. It does not promote devotional claims, article praise, the author's own priority statements, or historical conclusions into verified scientific findings.
investigations.limitations: Only one academic article was read; its author says detailed analysis of the astronomical works is outside the article's primary focus. The 2005 English edition is community-produced and has unverified front-matter claims. Rekhta's Urdu pages were inaccessible after a registration gate, so no direct Urdu collation was possible. First-edition date, newspaper sources, calculation accuracy, diagram interpretation, biography, and independent reception remain open. Earth's motion is treated here only as a historical debate topic, not as a live scientific controversy.
investigations.laterInfluence: Not assessed. No transmission, scholarly reception, or influence claim is made from the source material consulted in this bounded batch.
